Maladaptive Strategies.value: I force myself to think only positive thoughts
Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
Any form of physical contact with others

Negative Appraisals.value: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal of feared uncontrollable rage is not well supported by the rest of the profile. There are no corresponding trigger, threat, memory, or strategy items suggesting anger-driven reactivity, aggression risk, or conflict; the other appraisals instead center on shame and hopelessness after rape. This makes the rage item clinically discordant within the selected five components.

issues.item: Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
issues.explanation: The strategy of constant socialising is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile in this rape-related presentation. The selected triggers are solitary/sensory reminders (silence, outdoor smells, anniversary), and the appraisals are shame, suicidality, and feared rage. Constantly surrounding oneself with people does not connect clearly to these reminders and is somewhat at odds with body shame after rape, making it the least coherent avoidance/coping item here.

vignette:
Amina was a 74-year-old African woman who had spent most of her life working the land, and it was on the path back from the fields, with the smell of damp soil rising after rain and the evening air suddenly gone still, that she was attacked and raped. She described the assault as beginning in a stretch of quiet so complete that she could hear her own breathing and the rustle of her clothes against her skin; later, that same kind of silence in the house could make her whole body tighten before she understood why. The memory remained bound to the smells of earth and outdoor vegetation, so that even now the scent of freshly turned soil, especially at the farm where she still worked when her strength allowed, could pull her back with alarming force to the place where she had been overpowered. On the anniversary of the assault, too, she found herself bracing for the day before she had even left bed, as though her body had learned the date more faithfully than her mind wanted to.

In the weeks after the rape, Amina tried to push away any thought that might bring back what had happened. She told herself repeatedly that she must keep her mind on “good things only,” forcing positive thoughts over the images that came without invitation, but the effort left her feeling false and strangely alone with it all. She began avoiding being in the dark and steering clear of circumstances that reminded her of the assault, especially the fields at dusk or any place where silence settled too heavily around her. She also drew back from being touched by anyone, including her partner, because even a hand on her shoulder could make her feel exposed and unsafe. Yet the more she pushed herself to stay cheerful and not dwell on it, the more she felt she had to lock away the parts of herself that were frightened, angry, and grieving; over time, that self-command hardened into another painful thought, that her life might no longer be worth living if this was what remained of it.

Amina came to believe that what had happened to her body had made her dirty, and that belief sat close to her shame. She spoke quietly about feeling contaminated, as if the assault had left something on her that washing could not remove. When she looked at herself, she no longer saw simply an older woman who had worked hard all her life; she saw someone diminished and altered in a way she could not undo. That shame fed her determination to avoid touch even more completely, because contact now felt like proof that others might sense what she feared was wrong with her. At the same time, the effort to stay only with positive thoughts and to keep away from painful reminders seemed to give these beliefs more room to grow in private. When she refused to let herself think about the rape directly, the feelings of dirtiness and bodily shame returned in a harsher form, filling in what she had tried to silence. And because she believed her body had been so violated, she became more sensitive to the very things that evoked the memory: the smell of earth from the fields, the darkening sky, and the abrupt hush that could fall around her home at night.

Over months, Amina’s life narrowed around these reactions. She still rose early, but her work in agriculture became harder because the outdoor smells that once belonged to ordinary labor now carried the assault with them, and she would tense or hurry away when the soil was wet and rich underfoot. At home, she arranged her evenings to avoid darkness and made sure there was noise in the room, because silence felt like the beginning of danger. She kept her distance from her partner, explaining it only as needing rest, though in truth she feared that any physical contact would pull her back into the same helplessness and disgust. The more she arranged her days around not being reminded, the more those reminders seemed to find her anyway, especially near the anniversary, when her mind returned to the event with a force she could not outthink. And each time she caught herself fighting the images by insisting on positive thoughts, she was left feeling that she had failed to master her own mind, which made her more certain that something in her was broken and that her life had already been reduced to endurance.

By the time she sought help, Amina was describing a heavy weariness and a growing fear that she could not keep living this way. What brought her in was not one single moment, but the accumulation of being startled by silence, recoiling from touch, and feeling herself shrink each time the smell of the earth or the approach of the anniversary reopened the wound. She said she wanted to believe she could still be whole, but what frightened her most was the thought that she might remain trapped between shame and emptiness, unable to feel clean, safe, or worth anything again.
